name: Glacial Tundra
geological_features: Subglacial lakes warmed by geothermal activity
Exposed tundra strips along the equatorial belt
Glacial moraines forming ridge systems at ice sheet margins
description: Glacial Tundra is a large ice world where continental glaciers cover most of the surface, their blue-white expanse broken only by narrow equatorial strips of exposed frozen ground. The ice sheets are kilometers thick in places, their weight pressing the underlying crust into deep basins. Along the margins, glacial moraines form ridge systems of compressed rock and gravel.

The thin atmosphere carries bitter cold across the tundra strips, where the temperature never rises above freezing. The sky is a pale, washed-out blue during the short days, and the long nights reveal spectacular aurora displays driven by the planet's interaction with its star's solar wind. The silence is immense, broken only by the deep groaning of shifting ice.

Subglacial lakes have been detected beneath the thickest ice sheets, warmed by residual geothermal activity. These isolated liquid water bodies host thriving microbial ecosystems that have evolved in complete darkness for millions of years. Each lake appears to contain a unique microbial community, separated from its neighbors by kilometers of solid ice.

Glacial Tundra's subglacial ecosystems represent a natural laboratory for studying evolution in isolation. The planet also offers abundant water resources and geothermal energy for any settlement willing to bore through the ice. Several research stations operate along the equatorial tundra, but the harsh conditions and remoteness limit permanent habitation to dedicated scientists and support staff.
